extracted.intended_audience: journalists, newsroom editors, and informed news consumers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for newsroom decisions about publishing leaked documents (vs enterprise reporting), weighing accuracy, public interest, context, and source bias. Focuses on how to frame, label, and accompany leaked material so the public can judge it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify piece as leaked document versus enterprise reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: The Steele Dossier wasn’t a reported scoop—it was a leaked document. If it had been an enterprise story, the issue of whether to publish should have centered around whether the story was accurate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether the material is a leak (document dump/unaltered source material) or an enterprise investigation; apply different standards and priorities accordingly. For enterprise reporting the primary test is accuracy and independent verification. For leaked documents, consider transparency and the value of public access to the material even when parts are unverified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurate headline and clear framing
rubrics_metrics.description: The actual headline was 'These Reports Allege Trump Has Deep Ties to Russia.' That’s an accurate summary of the dossier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a headline that accurately summarizes what the documents contain without asserting unverified allegations as fact. Avoid sensational or definitive phrasing when material is alleged/unverified; frame as allegation or report when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Label verification status explicitly
rubrics_metrics.description: The story included a two-sentence subhed, the second sentence of which was, 'The allegations are unverified, and the report contains errors.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prominently state whether the contents are verified, unverified, or contain known errors. Use clear disclaimers in subheads/lead paragraphs rather than burying caveats deep in the copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weigh public’s need to know/public interest
rubrics_metrics.description: If we really believe that a free and independent press is essential to self-government... we need to trust the self-governors, the public, to make sense of what is happening... the American people needed to know about the Steele Dossier, both for the truths it contained and because of the consequences of its falsehoods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the public-interest value of disclosure (e.g., matters affecting public officeholders, public safety, or democratic processes) and balance it against potential harms from falsehoods. Prefer transparency when public decision-making is materially affected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider timing relative to other disclosure channels
rubrics_metrics.description: When would the rest of us have been let in on the specifics of the story that many of these editors had been poring over for weeks or even months?... Would we have been told then?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether insiders already had access and were withholding specifics, and whether delaying publication would leave the public uninformed until some later, less transparent disclosure. Consider how publication timing might affect subsequent events (e.g., investigations, firings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextualize facts alongside leaked material
rubrics_metrics.description: We need to provide them with both the facts and the context to make those judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When publishing leaked documents, accompany them with explanatory reporting that clarifies what is known, what is unverified, relevant corroboration or contradiction, and the broader context so readers can judge significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scrutinize and disclose source motives and biases
rubrics_metrics.description: Yes, the allegations of the dossier deserved press scrutiny, but so did the self-interest of those who prepared it, along with those on whom they relied. It's always critical in good reporting to consider the biases and behavior of sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate and report on who produced or distributed the material, their possible motives (political, financial), and any conflicts of interest; make that information available to readers as part of the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reporting unverified salacious allegations as fact
rubrics_metrics.description: The pee tape and Cohen-to-Prague stories were very likely never true, and should surely never have been reported as if they were.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refrain from treating lurid or potentially reputationally damaging claims as established fact unless corroborated by reliable evidence. Clearly mark such claims as allegations and avoid gratuitous repetition that amplifies falsehoods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be skeptical of elite gatekeeping ('trust us' critique)
rubrics_metrics.description: The implicit premise is that all of us should trust a small, self-referential and largely homogenous group of political reporting insiders to know more than they are telling us, and to dole out to voters what they think we can responsibly handle at a time of the insiders’ choosing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Question norms that prioritize withholding material on the basis that only insiders should judge readiness; balance professional caution with democratic transparency. Consider whether secrecy by insiders serves legitimate verification needs or merely preserves control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclose newsroom conflicts of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosure: Since this column was originally written, BuzzFeed has become a client of my consulting business. BuzzFeed, of course, did not see the column before it was published, and had no input on the content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists and outlets should disclose financial or professional relationships that could influence coverage decisions. Make such disclosures prominent and specific so readers can assess potential bias.
